overview:
The phrase "Comparison with other Indian ontologies" invites us to place a specifically Jain ontology—structured around substances (dravya), qualities (guṇa), modes (paryāya), and the many-sidedness of reality (anekāntavāda)—in conversation with other major Indian systems of being. These include Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya–Yoga, various Vedānta schools, Mīmāṃsā, and Buddhist Abhidharma traditions. Each of these systems develops a distinct map of what exists, how it exists, and how it can be known, yet they share a common intellectual environment of debate, mutual critique, and conceptual borrowing.

Jain ontology begins from a pluralistic realism. Reality is composed of multiple, irreducible substances—most centrally jīva (sentient soul) and ajīva (non-sentient entities such as matter, space, time, motion, and rest). Each substance possesses infinite qualities and undergoes changing modes while retaining its identity. Anekāntavāda, the doctrine of non-one-sidedness, insists that any adequate description of reality must coordinate identity and difference, permanence and change, universal and particular. This is articulated through nayavāda (standpoints) and syādvāda (conditioned predication), which together provide a formal language for expressing how a single entity can be truly described in apparently divergent ways without collapsing into contradiction.

Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika ontology, by contrast, is a robust realist system that emphasizes discrete categories (padārtha) such as substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion (karman), universal (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), inherence (samavāya), and absence (abhāva). While Jain thinkers accept many of these categories in practice, they criticize Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika for subordinating identity to difference—treating particulars and their distinctness as ontologically primary. Jain authors argue that this risks fragmenting reality into isolated units and underestimates the complex, relational character of existence. At the same time, Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika philosophers challenge Jain anekāntavāda as flirting with contradiction, prompting detailed Jain responses that clarify the logical structure of conditional predication.

Sāṃkhya–Yoga presents another influential ontology, built around two ultimate principles: puruṣa (pure consciousness) and prakṛti (primordial materiality). Prakṛti evolves into a hierarchy of tattvas (principles) that constitute the empirical world, while puruṣa remains eternally distinct and inactive. Jain ontology shares with Sāṃkhya a concern to distinguish the conscious principle from material processes, but it resists the strict dualism of puruṣa and prakṛti. For Jains, each jīva is a distinct, embodied soul entangled with karmic matter (pudgala), and liberation involves the shedding of this karmic bondage rather than the mere recognition of a metaphysical duality. Ontologically, Jainism thus coordinates identity and difference across a richer field of substances, rather than reducing all materiality to a single prakṛti.

Vedānta ontologies, especially Advaita Vedānta, often serve as Jainism’s primary foil in debates about the nature of reality. Advaita posits a single, non-dual Brahman as the ultimate reality, with the empirical world understood as appearance (māyā) or illusory transformation (vivartavāda). From a Jain perspective, this is a philosophy of identity alone, which risks negating the reality of difference, plurality, and ethical relations. Jain thinkers argue that the world of many souls and diverse entities cannot be dismissed as mere illusion without undermining the very possibility of moral responsibility and spiritual progress. In response, some Vedānta schools (such as Viśiṣṭādvaita and Dvaita) develop qualified or dualistic ontologies that affirm real difference alongside unity, and Jain authors engage these systems as partial moves toward the Jain ideal of a coordinated synthesis of identity and difference.

Buddhist Abhidharma ontologies, especially in schools like Theravāda and Sarvāstivāda, analyze reality into momentary dharmas—fundamental events or factors that arise and cease in rapid succession. The doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) and the denial of a permanent self (anātman) represent, in Jain classification, a philosophy of difference alone. Everything is flux; there is no enduring substance underlying change. Jain philosophers critique this view as unable to account for continuity, personal identity, and the cumulative structure of karmic responsibility. Yet they also learn from Buddhist analytical rigor, incorporating fine-grained distinctions into their own accounts of karmic particles, mental states, and modes of consciousness.

Mīmāṃsā, while primarily concerned with Vedic ritual and hermeneutics, also offers an ontology that treats the Veda as eternal and authoritative, and that emphasizes the reality of dharma as a causal force linking ritual action to future results. Jain ontology shares with Mīmāṃsā a strong sense of moral causality, but grounds it in the concrete mechanism of karmic matter binding to the soul. Where Mīmāṃsā focuses on the ontological status of scriptural injunctions and ritual acts, Jainism focuses on the ontological status of karmic aggregates and the soul’s modifications.

Across these comparisons, a distinctive feature of Jain ontology is its meta-ontological reflexivity. Anekāntavāda does not merely add another list of entities to the Indian philosophical landscape; it offers a theory of how ontological claims should be made, qualified, and related to one another. Jain authors argue that many inter-school disputes arise from absolutizing a partial standpoint—taking one true aspect of reality (such as unity, plurality, permanence, or flux) and elevating it to the whole. By insisting on conditional, standpoint-sensitive predication, Jain ontology seeks to preserve the insights of other Indian systems while avoiding their one-sidedness. This makes Jainism both a participant in and a critic of the broader Indian ontological conversation.

Modern comparative scholarship has highlighted this Jain contribution by framing anekāntavāda as a sophisticated theory of "identity-in-difference" and by mapping Jain categories against Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika padārthas, Sāṃkhya tattvas, Vedānta’s Brahman–jīva–jagat triad, and Buddhist dharmas. Such work shows that Jain ontology is not an isolated schema but a dynamic, dialogical structure that evolved through centuries of debate with other Indian traditions. At the same time, it cautions against oversimplifying Jain pluralism as mere relativism or treating other ontologies as monolithic. Each system contains internal debates, revisions, and nuanced positions that must be respected when drawing comparisons.

In summary, the comparison with other Indian ontologies reveals Jainism as a pluralistic realist framework that coordinates identity and difference, substance and mode, permanence and change, and ethical and metaphysical concerns. Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya–Yoga, Vedānta, Mīmāṃsā, and Buddhist Abhidharma each offer powerful alternative maps of reality, but Jain ontology distinguishes itself by its many-sided method of description and its insistence that no single ontological emphasis can exhaust the complexity of what exists. This comparative lens deepens our understanding of Jain thought and situates it within the rich, contested field of Indian philosophical reflection on being.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: This is the meaning of reality.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārthasūtra is a foundational Jain philosophical text that systematically presents Jain ontology and epistemology. Its opening sūtra signals a concern with the "meaning of reality" (tattvārtha), and subsequent chapters classify substances (dravya), qualities (guṇa), modes (paryāya), and the categories of jīva and ajīva. In comparative work, Tattvārthasūtra often serves as the primary anchor for mapping Jain ontology against Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika padārthas, Sāṃkhya tattvas, and Buddhist dharmas, because it offers a concise, aphoristic summary of what exists and how it is structured.

primary_sources.title: Nayādhammakahāo (Nayadhammakahāṇaya) and related Anekāntavāda passages in the Āgamas
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Jain teachers within the Śvetāmbara canon
primary_sources.original_text: एगं लहं नयं न विण्णइ, बहु नयं विण्णइए
primary_sources.transliteration: egaṃ lahaṃ nayaṃ na viṇṇai, bahu nayaṃ viṇṇaiye
primary_sources.translation: One should not understand reality through a single, easy standpoint, but through many standpoints.
primary_sources.notes: Narrative and doctrinal passages in the Jain Āgamas introduce the idea that reality must be approached from multiple standpoints (naya). These early formulations of nayavāda and anekāntavāda underpin later, more technical treatments. In comparative ontology, such passages are crucial because they show that Jainism does not only list entities but also reflects on the method of describing them. This methodological emphasis distinguishes Jain ontology from more strictly categorical systems like Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and aligns it with broader Indian concerns about the limits of language and conceptualization.

primary_sources.title: Syādvāda-naya texts (e.g., works attributed to Mallavādin and later commentators)
primary_sources.author: Mallavādin and subsequent Jain logicians
primary_sources.original_text: स्यादस्ति, स्यादनास्ति, स्यादस्ति च नास्ति च, स्यादवक्तव्यः इति
primary_sources.transliteration: syād asti, syād nāsti, syād asti ca nāsti ca, syād avaktavyaḥ iti
primary_sources.translation: In some respect, it is; in some respect, it is not; in some respect, it both is and is not; in some respect, it is inexpressible.
primary_sources.notes: Syādvāda articulates a sevenfold scheme of conditioned predication that allows Jain ontology to express complex truths about entities without collapsing into contradiction. Each predication is qualified by "syāt" (in some respect). In comparative ontology, this scheme is often contrasted with Nyāya’s insistence on non-contradiction, Buddhist momentariness, and Vedānta’s claims about absolute reality. The text demonstrates how Jain ontology integrates logical, linguistic, and metaphysical concerns to handle identity and difference.

primary_sources.title: Nyāya-sūtra (for contrast with Jain ontology)
primary_sources.author: Akṣapāda Gautama (traditional attribution)
primary_sources.translation: From the true knowledge of means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, doubt, purpose, example, conclusion, members of inference, reasoning, ascertainment, debate, wrangling, cavil, fallacious reasons, quibble, refutation, and points of defeat, there is attainment of the highest good.
primary_sources.notes: The Nyāya-sūtra sets out an epistemological and ontological program that underlies the Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika categories of reality. In comparative ontology, this sūtra is often juxtaposed with Jain texts to show differing emphases: Nyāya focuses on correct inference and categorical clarity, while Jain ontology adds a many-sided method of description. The contrast helps illuminate how Jain thinkers both adopt and critique Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika ontological structures.

primary_sources.title: Sāṃkhya-kārikā (for contrast with Jain ontology)
primary_sources.author: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
primary_sources.original_text: दुःखत्रयाभिघाताज्जिज्ञासा तदभिघातके हेतौ। दृष्टे सापार्था चेन्नैकान्तात्यन्ततोऽभवात्॥
primary_sources.transliteration: duḥkhatrayābhighātāj jijñāsā tadabhighātake hetau | dṛṣṭe sāparthā cen naikāntātyantato ’bhavāt ||
primary_sources.translation: From the affliction by the three kinds of suffering arises the desire to know the means of their cessation. If that means were seen (in the world), this desire would be pointless, since what is seen is not permanent and absolute.
primary_sources.notes: The Sāṃkhya-kārikā introduces the dualistic ontology of puruṣa and prakṛti and the hierarchy of tattvas. In comparative work, this text is used to highlight how Sāṃkhya reduces material reality to a single evolving principle (prakṛti), whereas Jain ontology maintains a plurality of substances and emphasizes karmic matter as distinct from other forms of ajīva. The shared concern with suffering and liberation provides a bridge for comparison, while the differing ontological structures mark a clear contrast.

misconceptions.myth: Jain ontology is simply another list of categories like Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika and does not differ significantly from other Indian systems.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain ontology does classify substances and categories, its distinctive contribution lies in anekāntavāda, nayavāda, and syādvāda—meta-ontological tools that govern how entities are described from multiple standpoints. This makes Jain ontology not just a catalogue of what exists, but a theory of how ontological claims should be qualified and related, which differs markedly from the more rigid categorical structures of Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika.

misconceptions.myth: Anekāntavāda means that all views are equally true and that Jain ontology promotes a kind of relativism.
misconceptions.reality: Anekāntavāda does not claim that every view is true; it claims that reality is complex and that true descriptions capture different aspects under specific conditions. Jain ontology rejects contradictory or ill-founded claims and insists on disciplined, standpoint-sensitive predication. The doctrine is a structured pluralism, not an anything-goes relativism.

misconceptions.myth: Buddhist and Jain ontologies are basically the same because both reject a permanent, substantial self in the ordinary sense.
misconceptions.reality: Buddhist Abhidharma generally denies any enduring self (anātman) and analyzes reality into momentary dharmas, whereas Jain ontology affirms a plurality of enduring souls (jīvas) that are ontologically real but obscured by karmic matter. The two traditions share concerns about ignorance and suffering, but their ontological commitments about selfhood, continuity, and substance are fundamentally different.

misconceptions.myth: Advaita Vedānta and Jain ontology both ultimately deny the reality of the empirical world, so their differences are minor.
misconceptions.reality: Advaita Vedānta treats the empirical world as appearance (māyā) relative to the non-dual Brahman, whereas Jain ontology affirms the reality of the empirical world, its plurality of substances, and the moral significance of embodied existence. For Jains, denying the reality of difference and plurality would undermine karmic responsibility and the path of liberation. The divergence is therefore substantial, not minor.

misconceptions.myth: Sāṃkhya’s dualism of puruṣa and prakṛti is identical to the Jain distinction between jīva and ajīva.
misconceptions.reality: Although both systems distinguish a conscious principle from material processes, Sāṃkhya reduces all materiality to a single prakṛti, while Jain ontology recognizes multiple non-sentient substances (such as matter, space, time, motion, and rest) and treats karmic matter as a specific kind of pudgala. Jain jīva–ajīva duality is embedded in a broader pluralistic framework and cannot be equated straightforwardly with Sāṃkhya’s puruṣa–prakṛti dualism.
